content: 1. The estimated rifampicin needs for the next year in Country ABC are calculated based on the number of cases reported in the previous year and the expected number of contacts per index case. For example, with 847 cases and 40 contacts per case, the total expected contacts are 33,880. 2. In special situations, such as the blanket approach, the number of eligible individuals is estimated as the total population above two years of age in the area. If this data is unavailable, it can be derived from the total population. 3. A buffer stock of rifampicin may not be necessary, as not all contacts can be traced, some may refuse treatment, or others may not meet inclusion criteria. Coverage of 85-90% of the target population is considered excellent. If calculations are based on 100% coverage, the remaining 10-15% can serve as a buffer stock. 4. Age-wise rifampicin requirements should be calculated after determining the total required doses. This involves assessing the percentage of the population in different age groups, as contacts will be drawn from the community. For instance, approximately one-third of the population may weigh ≥20 kg, and the percentage of children aged 2-5 years can be estimated as half of the proportion of the 0-5 years age group. 5. Rifampicin needs for each age group can be calculated using the formula: rifampicin needs for age group = (% population of age group x total doses required) / 100. For example, in Country ABC, 52% of the population aged ≥15 years requires 17,618 doses, while 12% of the population aged 10-14 years requires 4,066 doses. 6. Rifampicin is available in 300 mg and 150 mg capsules. The total number of capsules required for each age group is calculated based on the number of contacts and the dosage per contact. For example, in Country ABC, 41,000 capsules of 300 mg and 8,000 capsules of 150 mg are needed for one year. 7. Injectable rifampicin is not recommended for prophylaxis. Syrup formulations, such as 60-ml bottles of 100 mg/5 ml, are preferred for younger children aged 2-5 years. 8. Drug supply management for rifampicin should follow standard practices for other medicines. Forecasting should account for annual requirements, and distribution can be done quarterly, biannually, or annually, considering factors like shelf life, transport availability, and accessibility. 9. Rifampicin should be stored in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight and children, following good storage practices. The first expiry/first out (FEFO) principle should be applied to maintain the supply chain. 10. Counseling for single-dose rifampicin (SDR) should address safety, side effects, and its usefulness. Before administration, active leprosy or tuberculosis must be ruled out, and contraindications such as liver or kidney involvement, age under two years, or pregnancy must be checked. 11. For individual contacts, counseling about the disease should be conducted after obtaining consent for disclosure. If consent is not provided, post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) with SDR should not be administered. 12. In the blanket approach, advocacy with local health or civil authorities is essential, and consent from the index case may not be required. Records of SDR administration, including name, age, address, date, and place, should be maintained. 13. Contact tracing and PEP should be routine components of the national leprosy program. Records should be minimal yet sufficient, aligning with routine data recording and reporting systems. Patient treatment cards should include consent for contact tracing and complete patient details. 14. Contact lists or registers should be introduced to document information about contacts, as this data is not directly relevant to the clinical management of the index case. These records can be maintained electronically with proper backup. 15. Reporting related to contact tracing and PEP should be integrated into the routine reporting system of the national leprosy program. Reporting frequency can align with existing leprosy reporting schedules, such as quarterly, monthly, or annually. 16. Preparations at the national level for contact tracing and PEP implementation include adapting technical guidance to the local context, developing recording and reporting formats, and ensuring advocacy with policymakers and the community. 17. National-level training of trainers should be organized to build capacity for contact tracing and PEP. These trainers can then cascade training to health staff and volunteers at lower levels. 18. Rifampicin for prophylaxis can be obtained through donation or procurement, following national policies. Distribution should ideally be planned alongside regular multidrug therapy (MDT) supplies. 19. Community awareness about the benefits of contact tracing and PEP should be raised through appropriate information, education, and communication (IEC) materials. 20. Preparations at the intermediate level (state, province, or region) include engaging stakeholders, organizing training sessions, and defining roles and responsibilities for health staff and community health volunteers. 21. Preparations at the peripheral level (district or community) involve similar activities, such as stakeholder engagement, training, and planning for contact tracing and PEP implementation. These activities should be embedded in regular leprosy control plans rather than creating standalone plans.
